title: UDLF deployment config — Splunk via contentctl
description: Optional, opt-in sub-schema for the `config` block of a UDLF deployment whose `platform` is `splunk-contentctl`. This is a different delivery path, not a different product: the deployer emits a contentctl-shaped detection YAML and hands it to the contentctl build pipeline (validate → build app → test), rather than building and uploading an app itself. Because contentctl owns the build, this block mirrors contentctl's own field names and nesting so the emitted file needs no translation. Two consequences follow. First, `type` is the real discriminator — it selects the ESCU default deployment (and therefore the schedule), decides whether RBA and notables are emitted at all, and gates several other fields. Second, contentctl models are `extra="forbid"` at every level, so this sub-schema is closed and offers no `advanced` passthrough: an unmodelled key would fail the contentctl build anyway. Fields UDLF already owns are deliberately absent — ATT&CK IDs and CVEs come from the top-level `threat` block, implementation and false-positive prose from `detection_context`, tests from the top-level `tests` array, analytic stories from strategy membership, and `nist` is overwritten by contentctl from `type` so authoring it has no effect. This schema is NOT referenced by the UDLF core schema; apply it separately when you want the block validated. There is deliberately no `severity` override here, unlike every other platform: contentctl's Deployment.alert_action.notable model carries only rule_title, rule_description and nes_fields, so a per-detection severity cannot be authored through contentctl at all. `detection_context.severity` still informs the detection; it simply has nothing to override.

then.$comment: contentctl rejects an rba block on Hunting and Correlation detections: their default ESCU deployments do not enable risk-based alerting, so any risk config would be silently dropped or raise. The inverse rule — rba is *required* for TTP and Anomaly — is gated on the detection being production, which lives outside this block (UDLF `lifecycle: live`), so it is a deployer-side check rather than a schema constraint.
Hunting detections are never enabled on install.

schema.description: Self-identifying sub-schema version for this config block, so this file can version independently of UDLF core as contentctl evolves.

type.description: contentctl analytic type — the discriminator for the whole block. It selects the ESCU default deployment by name (`ESCU Default Configuration <type>`), which supplies the schedule and alert actions, and it determines whether notables and RBA are emitted: TTP gets both, Anomaly gets RBA only, Hunting gets neither, Correlation gets a notable titled `RBA: <name>`. Because the schedule is inherited from the matched deployment, there is no `schedule` field here — override it with the `deployment` block below.

data_source.description: Names of the contentctl data sources this detection relies on. Each must resolve to an entry under the content pack's `data_sources/` directory. A single entry may join several sources with ` AND ` when the search correlates across them.

rba.description: Risk-Based Alerting. Valid only for `type` TTP and Anomaly — contentctl rejects it on Hunting and Correlation. For production TTP and Anomaly detections contentctl requires it with at least one risk object.

message.description: Risk and notable message template. Every `$field$` token must correspond to a field the search actually produces — contentctl validates this for production detections.
examples: A download cradle was executed on $dest$ by $user$

risk_objects.description: Entities that accrue risk. Score is per object, not per detection.

field.description: Search field holding the risk object. Must be present in the search.

score.description: Risk contributed each time the detection fires. contentctl caps this at 100, unlike raw Splunk ES.

threat_objects.description: Indicators associated with the risk event. May be empty, but contentctl requires the key to be present.

field.description: Search field holding the threat object. Must be present in the search.

type.description:
Category of the threat object. contentctl enforces this list and rejects anything outside it at build time — note there is deliberately **no `other` fallback**, so a contentctl deployment cannot express an unrecognised threat object type at all. That is faithful to contentctl: its ThreatObjectType has 26 members and no OTHER/UNKNOWN. If you need a type outside this list, the value cannot ship through contentctl.

These spellings are contentctl's own and differ from the Splunk RBA community list (`ip_address` here versus `ip` there, `domain` versus `url_domain`). contentctl writes the value verbatim into savedsearches.conf, so it is what a running ES instance will contain. The `splunk-es` sub-schema accepts both vocabularies for exactly this reason; do not rewrite between them when a detection carries both deployments.

drilldown_searches.description: Drilldown searches surfaced with the alert. contentctl requires at least two for production detections other than Hunting, one of which must contain the `%original_detection_search%` placeholder — that rule is gated on lifecycle, which lives outside this block, so it is enforced by the deployer rather than here. Omit entirely to let contentctl generate defaults from the risk objects.

search.description: Drilldown SPL. May contain `%original_detection_search%`, substituted with the detection's own search at build time.

earliest_offset.description: Start of the drilldown window. contentctl requires this key explicitly — it has no default. Commonly `$info_min_time$`.

latest_offset.description: End of the drilldown window. contentctl requires this key explicitly — it has no default. Commonly `$info_max_time$`.

enabled_by_default.description: Whether the saved search is enabled when the app is installed. contentctl permits `true` only for production TTP, Anomaly, and Correlation detections. Distinct from the UDLF deployment `mode`, which describes intended runtime behaviour rather than install-time state — a deployment may be `mode: alert` and still ship disabled for the customer to switch on.

explanation.description: Longer-form text shown in the ES Use Case Library, where that should differ from the detection's description. Omit to let contentctl fall back to the description derived from `detection_context.description`.

tags.description: contentctl's tags block, mirroring its nesting so the emitted YAML needs no restructuring. Only the tags UDLF does not already own appear here — ATT&CK IDs and CVEs come from the top-level `threat` block, and analytic stories from strategy membership.

asset_type.description: Type of asset the detection targets. contentctl enforces this closed list.

security_domain.description: ES security domain the detection belongs to.

product.description: Splunk products the detection is valid for.

group.description: Arbitrary grouping labels used by the content pack.

atomic_guid.description: Atomic Red Team test GUIDs this detection covers. Each must match an `auto_generated_guid` in the Atomic Red Team catalogue.

throttling.description: Alert suppression. Note the narrower period syntax than raw Splunk — contentctl allows seconds, minutes, and hours only, not days.

fields.description: Fields to suppress on. Each must appear in the search, and none may contain a space — contentctl errors on spaces because the conf value is comma-delimited and unquoted.

period.description: Suppression window in seconds, minutes, or hours. Days are not accepted — express one day as `86400s`, `1440m`, or `24h`.

manual_test.description: Reason this detection cannot be tested automatically. Setting it makes contentctl skip the detection's tests rather than fail the build for missing them, so it should explain why rather than merely assert the fact.

event_schema.description: Event schema the search is written against.

mappings.description: Custom field mappings. Loosely typed by contentctl and passed through unvalidated.

deployment.description: Inline deployment override. Normally omitted: contentctl resolves the schedule and alert actions by matching `type` to one of the five built-in ESCU deployments. Supplying this block forces contentctl to build an Embedded deployment for this detection alone, overriding the type-based default. Use it only when this detection genuinely needs a different schedule or alert action from every other detection of its type.

scheduling.description: Schedule override. contentctl requires all four keys when the block is present.

cron_schedule.description: Cron expression for the saved search.

earliest_time.description: Start of the search window as a Splunk relative-time modifier.

latest_time.description: End of the search window as a Splunk relative-time modifier.

schedule_window.description: How far the scheduler may delay the search.

alert_action.description: Alert action override. Only `notable` and `rba` are implemented by contentctl — its `email`, `slack`, and `phantom` models exist but raise at serialize time, so they are excluded here rather than modelled as traps.

notable.description: Notable event settings. contentctl requires all three keys when the block is present.

rule_title.description: Notable title. The built-in deployments use the literal `%name%`, substituted with the detection name at build time.

rule_description.description: Notable description. The built-in deployments use the literal `%description%`.

nes_fields.description: Notable Event Suppression fields offered to the analyst.

rba.description: Whether risk-based alerting is emitted. This is only the on/off switch — the risk objects themselves live in the top-level `rba` block of this config.

enabled.description: Turn RBA on for this detection. contentctl emits risk output only when true.
